1.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Human retinas require 20 to 30 minutes in darkness to build rhodopsin night vision, while red LED light preserves dark adaptation.
core_mechanism_bullets: 1. Refractor (Objective Lens at Front): Convex glass objective bends starlight to a rear focus; sealed low-maintenance tube ideal for lunar and planetary crispness.
2. Newtonian Reflector (Primary Mirror): Parabolic rear mirror reflects light to a 45-degree flat diagonal mirror and side eyepiece; zero chromatic color fringe.
3. Catadioptric (Compound Lens + Mirror): Folds a long focal length into a compact portable tube using a front corrector plate and curved secondary mirror.
4. Magnification Formula: M = F_obj / F_eye: A 1,200 mm focal-length Dobsonian with a 25 mm eyepiece yields 48x wide-field views (swap to 10 mm for 120x).
1.worked_field_example: A single 1-second glance at an unfiltered white smartphone screen bleaches rod photopigments and resets the 30-minute adaptation clock.
1.counselor_tabletop_demo: Cover a flashlight lens with red filter tape and practice reading a circular star planisphere without using white light.
1.real_world_connection_box: NASA Night Sky Network & DarkSky Field Standard: Human retinas require 20 to 30 minutes in darkness to build rhodopsin night vision, while red LED light preserves dark adaptation.

2.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Surface temperature governs star color across the O-B-A-F-G-K-M sequence from hot blue stars above 30,000 kelvins to cool red stars near 3,000 kelvins.
core_mechanism_bullets: Class O & B: Hot Blue-White (10,000-40,000 K): Massive short-lived supergiants like Rigel and Spica that fuse fuel rapidly and end as core-collapse supernovae.
Class A & F: Crisp White (6,000-10,000 K): Bright familiar guideposts including Sirius (brightest night star at 8.6 light-years), Vega, and Procyon.
Class G: Yellow Main Sequence (5,200-6,000 K): Our Sun (G2V, 5,778 K photosphere) steadily fuses hydrogen into helium across a 10-billion-year lifespan.
Class K & M: Orange-Red Stars (2,400-5,200 K): Includes cool red supergiants (Betelgeuse, Antares) and long-lived red dwarfs like Proxima Centauri (4.24 ly).
2.worked_field_example: In Orion, blue-white Rigel burns near 12,000 kelvins while red supergiant Betelgeuse glows cooler near 3,500 kelvins.
2.counselor_tabletop_demo: Point out hot blue-white Rigel and cool orange-red Betelgeuse on a winter sky chart to see stellar surface temperature with the naked eye.
2.real_world_connection_box: NASA Astrophysics & IAU Stellar Classification Standard: Surface temperature governs star color across the O-B-A-F-G-K-M sequence from hot blue stars above 30,000 kelvins to cool red stars near 3,000 kelvins. Sun-like stars evolve into red giants and white dwarfs, whereas massive stars end in core-collapse supernovae.

3.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Light-gathering power scales with the square of objective aperture diameter.
core_mechanism_bullets: Synodic Lunar Cycle (29.53 Days): New -> Waxing Crescent -> First Quarter -> Waxing Gibbous -> Full -> Waning Gibbous -> Third Quarter -> Waning Crescent.
Solar Eclipse (New Moon Alignment): Moon's dark Umbra cone traces a narrow ~100-mile path of totality across Earth; Penumbra sees a partial eclipse.
Lunar Eclipse (Full Moon in Earth Shadow): Earth's atmosphere refracts sunset-red wavelengths onto the eclipsed Moon ('copper Moon'); 100 percent safe with naked eyes.
CRITICAL ISO 12312-2 Solar Eye Safety: NEVER look at the un-eclipsed or partially eclipsed Sun through unfiltered binoculars, telescopes, or sunglasses!
3.worked_field_example: An 8-inch reflector collects four times as much starlight as a 4-inch lens, and a 1,200 mm focal length with a 25 mm eyepiece yields 48x power.
3.counselor_tabletop_demo: Trace light rays through the refractor lens, Newtonian parabolic mirror, and Schmidt-Cassegrain folded tube on the optical cutaway.
3.real_world_connection_box: NASA & Astronomical League Telescope Optics Standard: Light-gathering power scales with the square of objective aperture diameter. Telescope magnification equals objective focal length divided by eyepiece focal length.

4.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Human retinas require 20 to 30 minutes in darkness to build rhodopsin night vision, while red LED light preserves dark adaptation.
core_mechanism_bullets: 1. Protect Dark Adaptation (Red LED Only): Cover flashlights with deep red film and switch phones to red-filter mode so rhodopsin chemical sensitivity stays intact.
2. Cut Skyglow & Trespass Light (Req 1c): Use full-cutoff downward outdoor fixtures with warm 2700K bulbs and motion timers to preserve starry skies and wildlife.
3. Star-Hopping Angular Hand Gauge: At arm's length: pinky tip = 1 deg, 3 middle fingers = 5 deg, closed fist = 10 deg, outstretched handspan = 20 deg.
4. Thermal Acclimation & Dew Shield: Set telescope outdoors 30 minutes before observing so tube currents stabilize, and extend dew shield against lens fogging.
4.worked_field_example: A single 1-second glance at an unfiltered white smartphone screen bleaches rod photopigments and resets the 30-minute adaptation clock.
4.counselor_tabletop_demo: Cover a flashlight lens with red filter tape and practice reading a circular star planisphere without using white light.

6.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Solar eclipses occur at New Moon inside the lunar umbra, and lunar eclipses occur at Full Moon inside Earth's shadow.
core_mechanism_bullets: Class O & B: Hot Blue-White (10,000-40,000 K): Massive short-lived supergiants like Rigel and Spica that fuse fuel rapidly and end as core-collapse supernovae.
Class A & F: Crisp White (6,000-10,000 K): Bright familiar guideposts including Sirius (brightest night star at 8.6 light-years), Vega, and Procyon.
Class G: Yellow Main Sequence (5,200-6,000 K): Our Sun (G2V, 5,778 K photosphere) steadily fuses hydrogen into helium across a 10-billion-year lifespan.
Class K & M: Orange-Red Stars (2,400-5,200 K): Includes cool red supergiants (Betelgeuse, Antares) and long-lived red dwarfs like Proxima Centauri (4.24 ly).
6.worked_field_example: Over each 29.5-day synodic cycle, the Moon progresses through eight sunlit phases without an eclipse on most months due to its 5-degree tilt.
6.counselor_tabletop_demo: Use a flashlight (Sun), baseball (Earth), and marble (Moon) tilted 5 degrees to model all eight lunar phases and nodal eclipses.
6.real_world_connection_box: NASA Eclipse Science & AAS Orbital Standard: Solar eclipses occur at New Moon inside the lunar umbra, and lunar eclipses occur at Full Moon inside Earth's shadow. Because the Moon's orbit is tilted 5 degrees to Earth's ecliptic plane, eclipses happen only when syzygy aligns with an orbital node.
